Peter, I appreciate the payroll experience behind your view. You’re right that an informal, repeatable advance can leave people relying on next month’s pay, create recovery problems when someone leaves, and quietly turn HR into a lending desk. I also agree that financial literacy and clearer access to SACCO services are worth pursuing.

I’d be cautious, though, about assuming that giving notice and pointing people to a SACCO means they’ll adjust without wider consequences. We tried almost exactly that at my employer in 2025. We gave two months’ notice, closed advances, and held a financial-literacy session with the SACCO. Six months later, reception had logged 61 calls from debt collectors and loan apps. Some callers were contacting supervisors who had been listed as referees. We also saw more unplanned absence in the two days after month-end; our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers trying to sort out loans.

That doesn’t prove that every call or missed run was caused by closing advances, and I wouldn’t present it as a controlled study. But it was enough to challenge our assumption that the change would be painful for a couple of pay cycles and then resolve itself. People still had urgent expenses. A SACCO loan that takes two or three weeks and needs guarantors may be a good option for planned borrowing, but it may not help when a child is sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday.

One case has stayed with me: a loader at our Changamwe depot had taken loans from six apps by the time he came to me, borrowing from one to repay another. It took four months of work with payroll to help unwind the situation. That isn’t an argument that employers should replace SACCOs or banks, or cover every shortfall. It is a reminder that closing the company option doesn’t necessarily remove the need; it can move the problem into places that are harder for the employee and the business to see.

We reopened advances in September 2025, but changed them from an informal favour into a written policy. The rules are simple: no more than 40% of net pay, once per pay cycle, repaid in full through the next payroll, with no fee. Requests go through the payroll portal, not my office. Before approving one, we check that total deductions stay within the Employment Act limit of two-thirds of wages. The 40% cap is our own policy limit, not the legal one; it gives us a tighter boundary and helps ensure that no one is left with nothing at month-end.

Since reopening, we’ve received about 55–70 requests a month, averaging roughly KES 9,000. We’ve recovered everything except from two employees who left; total write-offs for the year were about KES 14,000. That is not zero risk, and the figures come from a different workforce, so Brenda would need to test what is realistic for a 210-person processing firm. But they give us something more concrete than either “everyone will adjust” or “we have to approve whatever people ask for.” Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme because its maximum exposure is forecastable: there is a fixed ceiling, not an unpredictable commitment.

I think the strongest proposal for your meeting on the 18th may be a time-limited, controlled policy rather than a defence of the current informal arrangement. For example, you could propose:

- A written maximum tied to net pay, with a clear affordability check against statutory deduction limits.
- One request per pay cycle, with the full amount recovered through the next payroll and no fee.
- A standard request and approval route through payroll or a portal, with clear eligibility and recording rules.
- A defined overall ceiling or budget for Finance to forecast, plus a review after three or six months.
- A route for repeat requests to trigger a private check-in or referral to financial counselling—not automatic approval, and not a substitute for addressing persistent hardship.

You could compare the expected administration time and any likely write-offs with the costs you can actually track if employees are scrambling elsewhere: reception and supervisor time, absence after payday, missed production or delivery work, and payroll disruption. Those costs may be spread across departments, so they’re easy to overlook beside the visible line on a Finance forecast. I’d be careful to label estimates as estimates and avoid claiming the advances caused every absence or call.

Your Finance Manager is right to ask whether monthly requests are becoming a pattern, and Peter is right that recovery from leavers and HR workload matter. A policy should tackle those risks directly, rather than pretend they aren’t there. In our case, the experiment that changed our minds wasn’t “advances are always good.” It was that shutting the scheme without a measured alternative didn’t make the underlying need disappear.

Brenda, you’ll know your workforce and cash position best. But you may be able to go into the meeting with a proposed cap, repayment rule, approval route, and review date—and ask Finance to assess that bounded exposure alongside the costs of removing the option. That turns the discussion from whether the company should be a bank into whether a small, predictable emergency provision is safer than leaving people to find urgent money elsewhere.
